preamble: Close [u] is laxed to near-close [ʊ], usually as a short or closed-syllable variant. In English, short Middle English /u/ became lax /ʊ/ (pullen /ˈpulən/ > pull /pʊl/), and long /uː/ from the Great Vowel Shift was later shortened to /ʊ/ in good and foot. In Javanese /u/ is [ʊ] in closed syllables (kuru [kuru] 'thin', mung [mʊŋ] 'only').

examples.note: Roger Lass dates the laxing of short /u/ to /ʊ/ to the 17th century; other scholars date it earlier. Where /ʊ/ was not protected by a neighbouring labial or a following /l ʃ tʃ/ it later unrounded to /ʌ/ (FOOT–STRUT split).

examples.from: Early Modern English good /uː/ (< Middle English /oː/)
Early Modern English foot /uː/ (< Middle English /oː/)
examples.note: A later shortening of /uː/ to /ʊ/ in a handful of words; earlier-shortened blood and flood went on to /ʌ/.

Western Javanese keeps [u] and Eastern Javanese has [ɔ] in closed final syllables. This follows the six-vowel analysis of Javanese, in which [ʊ] is an allophone of /u/; Wiktionary writes it inside phonemic slashes.

sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Phonological history of English close back vowels. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonological_history_of_English_close_back_vowels
